title: Why a Variable Inside a Function Isn't Visible Outside
excerpt: Understand local and global scope, why assigning inside a function does not change outside variables, and how to avoid global.

headings.text: Variables Born Inside a Function Stay There
Assigning Inside a Function Creates a New Local
The global Keyword, and a Better Way
One More Gotcha: Hiding a Built-in Name

html:
You set a variable inside a function, call the function, and then try to use the variable. Python says it does not exist. Or the opposite: you change a variable inside a function and the change seems to vanish. Both surprises come from the same rule.

Scope decides where a variable can be seen: a variable created inside a function exists only inside that function. This lesson walks through the rule with short experiments, so you can predict what Python will do instead of guessing.

Variables Born Inside a Function Stay There

def make_total():
    total = 10 + 5
    return total

print(make_total())
print(total)
15
NameError: name 'total' is not defined

The call printed 15, but the next line failed with a NameError: Python does not recognise that name here. The name total was created while the function ran and thrown away when it finished. This is called a local variable. The only way to get a function's result out is to return it, as the first print did.

Functions Can Read Outside Variables

Can a function see variables defined outside it? Yes. A variable created at the top level of your program is global, and functions can read it:

rate = 0.25

def add_tax(price):
    return price + price * rate

print(add_tax(200))
250.0

Assigning Inside a Function Creates a New Local

Reading is easy. The trap is assigning. As soon as a function assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local to the function, even if a global with the same name exists:

counter = 0

def reset():
    counter = 99
    print("inside:", counter)

reset()
print("outside:", counter)
inside: 99
outside: 0

Why did the change not stick? Because counter = 99 inside the function made a brand new local variable that happens to share a name. The global counter was never touched. The same rule explains a more confusing error:

def increase():
    counter = counter + 1

increase()
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'counter' where it is not associated with a value

Because the function assigns to counter, Python decides the name is local to the whole function. The counter on the right of the = is then read before the new local counter has been given a value, which is what an UnboundLocalError reports.

The global Keyword, and a Better Way

If you really want a function to change a global variable, declare it with global:

counter = 0

def increase():
    global counter
    counter = counter + 1

increase()
increase()
print(counter)
2

It works, but functions that quietly change global variables are hard to follow and hard to test. A cleaner habit is to pass the value in and return the new one:

def increase_by_one(value):
    return value + 1

counter = 0
counter = increase_by_one(counter)
counter = increase_by_one(counter)
print(counter)
2

Functions Inside Functions

A function defined inside another function can read the outer function's variables. Python searches for a name from the inside out: first the function itself (local), then any enclosing function (the function this one is written inside), then the global scope, and finally the built-in names such as print:

def outer():
    message = "from outer"

    def inner():
        print(message)

    inner()

outer()
from outer

One More Gotcha: Hiding a Built-in Name

The built-in names are the last place Python looks, so any name you create earlier in the search can hide them. A classic example is naming a variable list:

list = [1, 2, 3]
list("abc")
TypeError: 'list' object is not callable

The name list now points to your data, not to the built-in function, so list("abc") tried to call a list as if it were a function; "not callable" in the message means exactly that. Deleting your variable with del brings the built-in back:

del list
print(list("abc"))
['a', 'b', 'c']

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonVariableScope.ipynb.

Summary

  • A variable created inside a function is local and disappears when the function ends; return values to get them out.
  • A function can read global variables.
  • Assigning to a name inside a function creates a new local variable, even if a global has the same name.
  • global name lets a function change a global, but passing values in and returning results is usually clearer.
  • Python looks up names from the inside out: local, enclosing function, global, built-in.
  • Avoid naming variables after built-ins such as list, str or sum, because your name hides the built-in.
